Allis shad (Alosa alosa) is a large anadromous clupeid that once supported major fisheries across Western Europe. Field surveys conducted in the Gironde-Garonne-Dordogne catchment have recorded individuals attaining a maximum total length of approximately 70 centimeters [Li = approximately 70 centimeters], placing this species among the largest members of the genus Alosa. Recent ichthyoplankton surveys during spring spawning runs indicate that freshly spawned eggs measure roughly 3 millimeters in diameter, and the resultant wet weight at birth for newly emerged prolarvae has been calculated accordingly at 0.0141 grams [Wwb = 0.0141 grams]. This modest starting mass contrasts sharply with the substantial growth trajectory the species undergoes during its marine phase. Comparative data from long-term mark-recapture studies suggest that the ultimate wet weight reached by fully grown adults can approach 4492 grams [Wwi = 4492 grams], a value reflecting the extensive lipid reserves required to fuel the long upstream migration and the energetically demanding process of gonadal maturation before spawning.

Under controlled laboratory conditions held at a constant water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], investigators have documented a maximum reproductive output of approximately 548 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 548 eggs per day] for gravid females during the peak of the spawning season. This elevated daily fecundity is consistent with the species' life history strategy as a batch spawner, where multiple clutches are released over a period of several weeks. The thermal regime was chosen because it closely approximates the mean river temperatures encountered by the fish during their spring ascent into freshwater spawning grounds. Under these same conditions, the maximum lifespan recorded for captive-reared individuals was 3285 days [am = 3285 days], a longevity that underscores the repeated spawning opportunities available to this iteroparous species over its protracted adult phase in the marine environment at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C].

Sexual maturation in this species exhibits a pronounced difference between the sexes, a pattern documented during a multi-year study of the spawning population in the River Adour. When maintained at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the time since birth at puberty for males was determined to be approximately 1642 days [tp = approximately 1642 days], whereas their female counterparts required a substantially longer developmental period, reaching puberty at about 2007 days since birth [tp = about 2007 days since birth]. This sexual dimorphism in maturation timing is typical of many large anadromous clupeids and likely reflects the greater energetic investment females must make in vitellogenesis and egg production before their first spawning event. The earlier maturation of males may confer a selective advantage by allowing them to secure prime spawning territories and achieve reproductive experience before competing with larger, older individuals later in the spawning run.

The pronounced difference in the time since birth at puberty between the sexes is a key demographic parameter influencing population dynamics. At 15 °C [T = 15 °C], female Allis shad undergo puberty after roughly 2007 days [tp = roughly 2007 days], a delay that considerably extends the generation time relative to the male maturation schedule of approximately 1642 days [tp = approximately 1642 days] under the same thermal conditions. This protracted juvenile phase for females is hypothesized to be linked to the accumulation of sufficient body reserves to sustain the high metabolic demands of egg production and the arduous upstream migration. Detailed otolith microchemistry analyses of returning adults have confirmed that the majority of females do not spawn for the first time until their sixth or seventh year, a pattern that makes the population particularly vulnerable to fishing pressure on the older age classes.

Basal life history traits such as the maximum total length of 70 centimeters [Li = 70 centimeters], combined with the ultimate wet weight of 4492 grams [Wwi = 4492 grams] in fully grown adults, place Allis shad at the upper end of the size spectrum within the Clupeidae. The population-level consequences of this large body size and delayed maturation are numerous and have direct implications for conservation management. The wet weight at birth of 0.0141 grams [Wwb = 0.0141 grams] is typical for a pelagic-spawning clupeid with small, buoyant eggs, but the subsequent larval and juvenile mortality rates in the estuary are extremely high. With a maximum lifespan of 3285 days [am = 3285 days] and a daily reproductive rate at 15 °C [T = 15 °C] of 548 eggs per day [Ri = 548 eggs per day], the species relies on a combination of high fecundity, iteroparity, and a long adult life to compensate for the enormous losses experienced during the early life stages in the planktonic environment.
